title: Capacity: Workers, Connections, and File Descriptors
intro: nginx handles thousands of connections per worker without much CPU, so it rarely runs out of processing power. It runs out of slots: connections per worker, and open files per process. Those limits are set in three different places, and the lowest one wins. You're on web-1 ahead of a sale expected to triple traffic.

steps.prompt: See the worker settings in the effective configuration: search it for lines starting with worker_.
steps.explanation: One worker per CPU core (auto), and 768 connections per worker.
steps.why: Maximum connections is workers times worker_connections: on 4 cores, 3,072. As a reverse proxy each client request uses two connections, one to the client and one to the upstream, so that's about 1,500 concurrent requests. 768 is a distribution default and is low for a busy proxy. worker_processes auto is right; more workers than cores doesn't help.

steps.prompt: nginx can report its live connection counts through the stub_status page, enabled here on localhost at /nginx_status. Fetch it.
steps.fake_output:
Active connections: 2204
server accepts handled requests
 9120044 9118310 31204410
Reading: 12 Writing: 310 Waiting: 1882
steps.explanation: 2,204 active connections out of a maximum of 3,072, and 'handled' is lower than 'accepts'.
steps.why: accepts minus handled (1,734 here) is connections nginx accepted and then had to drop because a limit was reached; on a healthy server the two are equal. 'Waiting' is idle keep-alive connections, which still occupy slots. At 72% of the limit before a tripling of traffic, this server will run out. Export these numbers to monitoring; this page is what the Prometheus nginx exporter reads.

steps.prompt: Check whether the limit has already been hit: search /var/log/nginx/error.log for 'worker_connections are not enough' and count the matches.
steps.explanation: 1,734 times, matching the dropped connections exactly.
steps.why: nginx says so plainly when it runs out, at 'alert' level, but only in the error log; clients just see connections reset. Raising worker_connections is the obvious fix, and it has a dependency that catches people: each connection needs a file descriptor, and that's limited separately.

steps.prompt: Check the open-files limit that actually applies to a running worker. A worker's pid is 88120.
steps.explanation: The soft limit is 1,024 open files per worker; the hard limit is 524,288.
steps.why: This is the limit the process really has, whatever any config file says. With worker_connections at 4,096 and a limit of 1,024 files, nginx would fail with 'Too many open files' long before reaching its connection limit. /proc/<pid>/limits is the truth for a running process; 'ulimit -n' in your shell shows your shell's limit, which is irrelevant to a service started by systemd.

steps.prompt: The configuration has been changed: worker_connections 4096 and worker_rlimit_nofile 16384. Test it and reload in one line, reloading only if the test passes.
expected_commands: sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx
steps.fake_output:
nginx: the configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf syntax is ok
nginx: configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf test is successful
steps.explanation: The test passed, so the reload ran.
steps.why: '&&' runs the reload only if the test succeeds, which is the safe one-liner to put in deploy scripts. worker_rlimit_nofile lets nginx raise its own workers' file limit, up to the hard limit, without touching systemd settings. Set it to at least twice worker_connections, since a proxied request uses two descriptors, plus some for log and cache files.

steps.prompt: Verify it took effect on a new worker. The new worker's pid is 91004.
steps.explanation: The new workers have 16,384 file descriptors each.
steps.why: Checking the running process closes the loop: three settings (worker_connections, worker_rlimit_nofile, and systemd's LimitNOFILE) can each be the bottleneck, and only /proc shows the result. One more limit sits outside nginx: connections to a single upstream address use local ports, about 28,000 by default. Upstream keepalive, which reuses connections, is what keeps a busy proxy from exhausting them.
